title: Recommending Books
keyIdea: A good book recommendation is made for the reader, not for you. Start from what your friend already enjoys, then give a specific reason that names something real in the book (its genre, a theme, the author's style or how the plot is built). Compare it to a book they know, and never give away the ending.

kid: When you recommend a book, you are helping a friend choose what to read next. So start with them, not you. What did they enjoy last time? A friend who loved a detective story may want another puzzle. A friend who reads comics may want short chapters and pictures.

Next, give a real reason. 'It's good' or 'it's the best book ever' does not tell your friend anything. A specific reason names something in the book. You might say the clues are hidden so you can solve the case first, or that every chapter ends on a cliffhanger.

Comparing helps too. 'If you liked Storm Island, try Lost in the Snow, because both are about friends who must survive together.' That links the books by genre or theme, which is what your friend enjoyed. Page count and cover colour are not good links.

Last, keep the surprises. Do not say who the thief is or how it ends. You can hint, like 'You will never guess who did it!' A great recommendation says who the book suits, gives a real reason, compares it to another book, and has no spoilers.
adult: In the England National Curriculum, Year 5 and 6 pupils should be 'recommending books that they have read to their peers, giving reasons for their choices'. They should also identify and discuss themes and conventions across books and make comparisons within and across books. Recommending is where those reading skills become a real task with a real audience.

The most common mistake is recommending your own favourite to everyone, whatever they like. The next is praise without reasons ('it's amazing') or reasons about surface features such as length, cover or how fast you read it. Children also often retell the whole plot, ending included, because summary feels like explanation.

Good recommendations use the vocabulary of KS2 reading: genre (mystery, adventure, fantasy), theme (friendship, courage, loss), narrator and author's style, and plot structure such as cliffhangers. Ask your child to say why a feature matters to this reader, not just that it is there.

The lab uses made-up books and readers. Your child matches three friends to books that fit what they enjoy and sorts specific reasons from vague praise. They also spot spoilers, link pairs of books by genre or theme, and build a full four-part recommendation.

familyTip: At bedtime or in the car, take turns recommending a book or film to someone else in the family. The rule: you must say who it suits, give one specific reason and keep the ending secret. Listeners can ask 'What makes you say that?'

visual.caption: Helpful in a recommendation, or not? Drag each line, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: It is a mystery you can solve with the detective
If you liked The Missing Key, you'll like this
The narrator makes jokes all the way through
It suits anyone who likes funny animal stories

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match readers to books, sort real reasons from vague praise, spot spoilers, link books by theme and build a recommendation.

practice.prompt: Omar loved a fantasy book with dragons. Which book should you recommend?
choices: Another fantasy with magic and quests
A true book about football
Your favourite joke book
practice.hint: Start from what Omar already enjoyed, not from what you like.
practice.explain: Omar liked fantasy, so a fantasy with magic and quests is most likely to suit him. Your own favourite might not.

choices: The chapters end on cliffhangers, so you keep turning pages
It is really, really good
My friend said it was cool
practice.hint: A specific reason names something you can find in the book itself.
practice.explain: Cliffhangers are a real feature of how the book is built. 'Really good' and what a friend said do not tell the reader anything about the book.

practice.prompt: Your recommendation has {a} lines. {b} of them give away the ending. How many lines are left once you cut the spoilers?
practice.hint: Take the spoiler lines away from the total number of lines.
practice.explain: {a} - {b} = {=a-b}. Cutting spoilers keeps the surprise for your friend.

practice.prompt: You want to give your friend {t} specific reasons to read a book. You have written {n} so far. How many more reasons do you need?
practice.hint: Take the reasons you have written away from the number you want.
practice.explain: {t} - {n} = {=t-n}. Each reason should name something real in the book, like a narrator or a twist.

pool.prompt: Who should a book recommendation be built around?
choices: The person you are recommending to
You, the recommender
The author
pool.hint: Who is going to read the book next?
pool.explain: A recommendation helps someone else choose, so it starts with what they enjoy.

choices: In the end, the dog was the hero all along
The story is set on a farm
It is told by a girl called Rosa
pool.hint: Which line gives away what happens at the end?
pool.explain: Saying who turns out to be the hero gives away the ending. Setting and narrator tell the reader what the book is like without spoiling it.

choices: Both books are about standing up to a bully
Both books have yellow covers
Both books are 150 pages
pool.hint: Look for something the two stories share inside, like a theme.
pool.explain: Standing up to a bully is a shared theme, so a reader who liked one may like the other. Covers and page counts say nothing about the story.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a genre?
choices: Mystery
Friendship
Chapter 2
pool.hint: A genre is a kind of story, like adventure or fantasy.
pool.explain: Mystery is a genre. Friendship is a theme, and Chapter 2 is just part of a book.

pool.prompt: Ben says, 'Read this, it's awesome.' How could he make it better?
choices: Say what in the book makes it awesome
Say it louder
Tell the whole story
pool.hint: What would help his friend decide?
pool.explain: 'Awesome' is praise. Naming a feature, like a funny narrator or a twist you never see coming, gives a real reason.

pool.prompt: Mia loves scary stories. You loved a book about baking. What should you do?
choices: Find her a scary story you read and liked
Push the baking book anyway
Tell her not to read scary stories
pool.explain: Mia's taste comes first. Recommend a scary book you have read and can give reasons for.

pool.prompt: You give {r} specific reasons and {v} vague ones like 'it's good'. How many reasons actually help your friend?
pool.hint: Only specific reasons say something about the book.
pool.explain: Only the {r} specific reasons help; the {v} vague ones say nothing about the book.

choices: If you like mysteries, try this: the clues are hidden in plain sight, like in The Missing Key, and I won't tell you who did it
It's the best book ever, everyone loves it
The thief is the gardener, but it's still good
pool.hint: Look for who it suits, a reason, a comparison and no spoilers.
pool.explain: The first one has all four parts. The others are vague or give the ending away.

pool.prompt: You wrote recommendations for {f} friends. {k} of them gave away the ending. How many recommendations kept the surprise?
pool.hint: Take the ones with spoilers away from the total.
pool.explain: {f} - {k} = {=f-k}. Those are the ones that kept the ending a surprise.
